newsitem.title: FRANCE: Car bombs in Algiers boost Ramadan death toll.
newsitem.headline: Car bombs in Algiers boost Ramadan death toll.

text.p: Two car bombs rocked central Algiers in less than five hours on Tuesday, killing at least seven people and wounding 54 and bringing the death toll so far in the Moslem holy month of Ramadan to well over 150.

Algerian security forces, in a statement carried by the official Algerian news agency APS, said the second car bomb exploded on Tuesday evening near a children's merry-go-round the El Madania district and killed one person.
A more powerful car bomb exploded nearly five hours earlier in the Boulevard des Martyrs, killing at least six people and wounding 44, 10 of them seriously, the official statement said.
Residents told Reuters the Boulevard des Martyrs car bomb was exploded by remote control and wrecked a bus.
An Algiers-based doctor said the bus belonged to the defence ministry and was carrying military personnel. He did not elaborate.
The official statement did not give the identities of those killed in the bombings.

Political analysts believe the killings are a message to President Liamine Zeroual and Algerians that the Islamic fundamentalists are still a formidable force despite repeated claims by the government that it has crushed the guerrillas.
About 60,000 people have been killed since 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.

Some 157 people have been killed and more than 170 wounded since Ramadan began on January 10. Militant fundamentalists regard the month of fasting as the period of jihad -- holy war -- against the secular military-backed government.

Algiers residents said the guerrillas had posted leaflets in the Casbah saying there would be 50 bombs during Ramadan and the Armed Islamic Group (GIA) warned that the rebel faction would step up attacks during Ramadan.

"The war will continue and will be intensified during the month of Ramadan. We have the means and the men to punish all those who are not on our side," GIA leader Antar Zouabri said in a statement posted on the walls of some mosques in northern Algeria and quoted by El Watan newspaper.
Residents said military officers defused two booby-trapped cars set to explode in Algiers streets on Tuesday. More than 15 more bombs had been defused in the past three weeks, they said.

The merry-go-round is 150 metres (yards) from the Ryad el Feth landmark trade centre which harbours the Martyrs Memorial where foreign officials lay wreaths to honour the dead in the North African country's independence struggle.

The explosions brought to at least four the number of blasts in Algiers in three days. On Sunday a car bomb killed at least 21 people -- an Algerian newspaper put the toll as high as 42 killed and more than 100 wounded. A bomb exploded outside a school on Monday but caused no casualties.
More than 300 people have been killed in a series of bombings and massacres, mostly in Algiers and surrounding towns, since November.
The government sees the guerrillas as "a group of criminals and traitors bent to the destruction of the nation through a senseless war".

After Tuesday's bombings, state television showed ministers visiting disabled people and inaugurating sport stadiums and an Algiers-based diplomat said by telephone the clear message was that "despite the deadly bombings, business goes on as usual".
